questions.q: Why does QuantPricer's scope deliberately exclude American-style early exercise and a full yield curve?
options: Those features are impossible to implement in C++
A tightly scoped capstone that does two things correctly and well-tested is a stronger, more finishable portfolio piece than one that attempts everything
pybind11 cannot bind any function related to interest rates
Bonds and options cannot both exist in the same library
questions.explain: Deliberately narrowing scope protects the capstone's chance of being finished and done well, rather than left half-complete trying to cover every possible feature.

questions.q: In the layered architecture, why must the C++ pricing core avoid including any pybind11 headers?
options: pybind11 headers are not compatible with the C++17 standard
So the pricing core remains a plain, independently unit-testable C++ library, usable even without a Python interpreter running
Because pybind11 headers would make the code run slower at runtime
Because CMake cannot compile a file that includes pybind11.h
questions.explain: Keeping the pricing core free of pybind11 headers means it can be built, run, and unit-tested as ordinary C++ with no Python involved at all — the bindings layer is a separate, thin translation on top.

questions.q: Which of the following is written as a properly measurable requirement, in the style the kickoff lesson recommends?
options: "The library should feel fast to use."
"Pricing 100,000 options via the vectorized C++ path must be at least 20x faster than an equivalent pure-Python loop, measured with timeit."
"Users should be happy with the API."
"The code should be clean and well organized."
questions.explain: A measurable requirement states a number and how it will be checked (20x faster, measured with timeit) rather than a subjective adjective like 'fast' or 'clean.'

questions.q: Why does the public API expose functions like `price_european(spots, strikes, rates, vols, expiries)` that accept whole arrays, rather than a function that prices one option per call?
options: pybind11 cannot bind a function that accepts a single scalar
A single-call-per-option API would reintroduce the per-call boundary-crossing overhead that defeats the performance reason for writing the library in C++
NumPy arrays are required by Python syntax rules
Because bonds cannot be priced with scalar arguments
questions.explain: Lesson 34 covered why crossing the Python/C++ boundary per element can dominate runtime; a vectorized API lets the boundary be crossed once per batch, which is what actually delivers the performance requirement.

questions.q: What is the main risk of skipping a written requirements step and jumping straight into writing pricing code?
options: The code will not compile under any C++ standard
There's no way to later check whether the finished capstone actually met its correctness, performance, and usability goals
pybind11 requires a requirements file to exist before it will build
CMake will refuse to run without a requirements document
questions.explain: Without requirements stated as checkable numbers up front, there is nothing concrete to test or benchmark against later, which is exactly what the testing and benchmarking lesson needs to grade the finished project.
